items.title: Claude-maker Anthropic poised for $1.4tn stock market debut
items.summary: Anthropic started just five years ago an is now one of the biggest names in artificial intelligence.
items.content:
Anthropic is poised to hit a value of at least $1.4 trillion (£1.1 trillion) when it debuts on the public stock market.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company behind the popular chatbot Claude said it will price shares at $83 each when it lists on Thursday on the Nasdaq, a tech-focused stock exchange based in New York.

That price will make it one of the most highly valued companies in the world.

It will be the first US company focused exclusively on AI to go public, marking a crucial test for the fast-growing industry.

The AI firm said earlier this month it would likely offer its shares for between $70 and $78 each, which valued the company at up to $1.3tn.

But demand for Anthropic's stock debut - commonly referred to as its initial public offering, or IPO - is very high, according to one early investor in the company who spoke with the BBC on condition of anonymity.

The person said shares were more than 10 times oversubscribed ahead of the public listing, meaning demand for Anthropic shares exceeded the number of shares available.

If that turns out to be the case, Anthropic's valuation could quickly blow past its target on Thursday when trading begins.

Depending on how strong that demand is, Anthropic could even exceed the early market valuation of Elon Musk's SpaceX, which was the world's most highly valued stock debut when it went public with a value of $2.2tn in June.

However, in the weeks that followed, SpaceX shares fell significantly in price .

As it stands, Anthropic's listing will see the firm raise more than $68bn from its initial investors. It is also expecting another $26bn from private placements. So the total amount the company will raise is expected to be $94bn.

The amount of cash Anthropic has raised from its listing is already more than SpaceX raised in June .

OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and Anthropic's biggest rival, is expected to go public next year.

Until then, Anthropic will be the only public company in the US that is considered a true AI company, or one that was founded and built around AI tools and products for consumers and businesses.

There is excitement around Anthropic's listing, but also some concern from investors around its ability to generate revenue and profits going forward.

Yang Wang, a principle financial analyst with Counterpoint Research, said the central issue for Anthropic is whether its business "can keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations come due in the next couple of years.

"Nevertheless, it is not an everyday occurrence for public investors to gain direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity," Wang said.

While nearly every other major tech company is pouring huge amounts of money into the technology and infrastructure required for their own AI tools, they are built around social media or online retail or online search. AI tools and applications are secondary.

"Anthropic going public gives us a whole new window into what AI demand looks like," Marta Norton, who heads investment strategy at investment firm Empower, told the BBC.

The seven Anthropic founders who are about to become multi-billionaires

Anthropic was started by a group of co-founders , led by siblings Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei, all of whom left their work at OpenAI to start a new AI firm.

The company has carved itself out in the ongoing AI race as more focused on building the technology with safety top of mind.

It refused to comply with a demand by the US Department of Defense that Anthropic's tools be used in an essentially unrestricted way. And Dario Amodei has been outspoken in his belief that AI tools may soon be so powerful that they present a threat to human existence.

Nonetheless, the company is looking to grow quickly and gain more access to financing through the public markets in order to do so.

Norton said Anthropic going public now, in a time of market volatility comes down to the simple fact that the company needs access to more money.

"AI is financially demanding," Norton said. "The public markets open up the financial spigot a little bit more, and so the time has come."

But broader anxieties have started to grow about the AI industry's business model, which is built on expensive, reliant on in-demand computer chips, controversial data centres, and deals with other tech companies.

The Federal Reserve Bank has expressed concern about the rapid growth of AI-related debt being financed through "complex and opaque" structures, according to minutes from its October meeting to discuss a potential rate rise.

A few of the meeting's participants also noted that "AI-related exposures were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms".

Can Anthropic's record breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?

items.title: The seven Anthropic founders who are about to become multi-billionaires
items.summary: The AI company behind Claude is about to sell its shares on the US stock market - making its founders very rich.
items.content:
In the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars.

The company behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least.

Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at $83 each, it said on Wednesday.

At that price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $19.3bn (£14.7bn) each.

So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy?

In 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT.

He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him.

Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track , and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity.

Initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences.

Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI.

But he began to worry that some people within the company were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship.

Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious".

Dario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic.

She and her brother have always genuinely liked each other, she says, but the only thing she ever did first, was when he followed her in becoming vegetarian.

Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz, going on to work for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright.

She has also worked at financial services platform Stripe, where she was head of risk operations.

The 39-year-old is president of Anthropic, manages the executive team, and leads the firm's research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work.

Tom Brown, now 39, followed the Amodei siblings when they left to found their new venture.

He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI, and prior to that was at Google on its DeepMind project.

Brown established his entrepreneurial credentials co-founding an app called "Grouper" that helps set up drinks between groups of friends.

He has supported US President Donald Trump's stance on datacentres, arguing that they are "an enormous source of prosperity".

Now as chief compute officer at Anthropic he is responsible for how the company secures and uses its computing resources.

Jack Clark, is another arts graduate among the original start-up's founding members and the only one who is not from North America.

Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.

He was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he worked initially in communications, later becoming its policy director.

Now, 37, Clark is head of public benefit at Anthropic. He also leads the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank.

Jared Kaplan, 42, is chief science officer at Anthropic, and heads its technical research. He is also an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore.

His work on scaling laws - which describe mathematical patterns that show that bigger AI models trained on more data tend to be more consistent - has helped provide AI firms with a framework for predicting AI behaviour, according to Anthropic.

Chris Olah is described as "interpretability research lead" primarily focused on how AI models work with each other.

But according to the New York Times, Olah has spent much of the last year convening meetings with faith leaders from across the religious spectrum.

Described by the newspaper as "boyish" but with "the zeal of an evangelist" the 34-year-old is reportedly exploring the relationship between morality and AI.

He previously led interoperability research at OpenAI, and prior to that was a research scientist at Google Brain.

The Canadian left the University of Toronto early, but later secured a Thiel Fellowship of $100,000, which is a scholarship to help gifted people move into research without a degree.

Sam McCandlish, 36, takes less of a public-facing role than the other founders, but like them will own around 1.6% of the company after its shares go on sale. As a result he too will see his stake crystallise into a hugely valuable asset.

McCandlish is Anthropic's chief architect, and helps shape and implement the company's policy designed to mitigate the risks of AI. Prior to this he worked on safety at OpenAI.

He has a physics PhD from Stanford, and maths and physics degree from Brandeis University outside Boston.

items.title: Russian man accused of spying on US tech defence company that assists Ukraine
items.summary: The suspect followed employees and was found with fake US IDs and two Russian passports, prosecutors say.
items.content:
US investigators have arrested a Russian man who they say was recruited by Moscow to spy on employees of a technology and defence firm in California's Silicon Valley that has links to Ukraine.

Igor D'iu is accused of acting as an agent of a foreign government to conduct a spying operation in Palo Alto, near San Francisco.

He is also accused of stalking employees of the company and possessing falsified identity documents.

The company is not named in charging documents, but is described as a publicly traded technology and defence company that produces software used by Ukraine in its war with Russia. US prosecutors say the company was targeted by Russia due to its assistance to Kyiv.

"The allegations in this case describe a state-sponsored operation to target and harass employees of an American technology and defense company because of that company's assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia," said US Attorney for the Northern District of California Craig Missakian.

"We will not tolerate any efforts - by foreign governments or otherwise - to turn Silicon Valley into a base for foreign intelligence operations."

Prosecutors say that D'iu entered the US unlawfully via the Mexico border, after travelling there from Istanbul in June.

He was allegedly recruited through the Telegram encrypted messaging app. His handlers referred to Russia as "'the Motherland' and directed D'iu to gather information about the company because it was supplying weapons used against Russia in Ukraine".

On their instruction, he purchased computers, phones, wireless networking equipment and remote access software - tools he needed for his spy mission.

He then went to a coffee shop located near the company's offices in Palo Alto, where he photographed laptop screens of employees who were working there.

His handlers also allegedly "instructed him to position his laptop at designated locations near the company so they could remotely access it and attempt to collect information from company employees in the vicinity".

According to CBS News, the BBC's US partner, the company in question is Palantir Technologies. Palantir did not reply to a BBC request for comment.

D'iu also allegedly conducted surveillance of employees and their residences.

On 3 September, he followed a vehicle driven by one senior executive for nearly 30 miles. He fled after she drove to a police station. Police later obtained evidence that he had followed other employees' cars on previous days.

During the investigation, officials discovered identity cards that had been falsified - including a US passport, California ID card, and a Social Security card with the fake name "Hugo Landry Johns".

A raid on his home in October in East Palo Alto turned up two Russian passports, and a handwritten notebook that contained numerous home addresses of employees "family members' names, educational and employment histories, and assessments of their strengths and weaknesses", prosecutors say.

He faces two charges related his alleged work as a foreign agent, one charge of interstate stalking, and one count of fraud related to his identity documents. He faces over 15 years in prison if found guilty.

Ukraine's long-range drones using Western tech to hit Russia

He has been held in jail since 2 November. It is unclear whether he has hired a lawyer who can speak on his behalf.

The arrest comes as espionage allegations roil the US tech industry, amid the news that Nvidia ex-CEO Jensen Huang had a romantic affair with a woman suspected of spying for China.

Last month, a former OpenAI employee was charged with planting a listening device in a company office. The man was later accused of having "considerable support" from the Saudi government.

items.title: Myanmar faces historic genocide verdict at UN court over Rohingya massacres
items.summary: No state has ever been found guilty by an international court of committing genocide.
items.content:
When the judges of the International Court of Justice read out their verdict in the seven-year-old genocide case filed by The Gambia against Myanmar on Thursday, they could make history.

In the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in 1948, after the Nazi Holocaust, dozens of individuals have been successfully prosecuted for the crime of genocide, in conflicts such as those in Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia.

But no state has ever been found guilty by an international court of committing genocide.

"It would be a judgment of landmark importance if The Gambia were to win this case," says Arsalan Suleman, the lawyer leading the case against Myanmar at the court. "It would give renewed vitality to the 1948 Genocide Convention and to the notion of international legal accountability for crimes committed by a state."

The mass expulsion of the Rohingya population of Rakhine State in August and September 2017 was without question a military operation of exceptional brutality.

I was among a very small number of journalists who witnessed the deliberate burning of Rohingya villages in Rakhine, and also the dreadful human suffering of the hundreds of thousands who fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.

Their accounts of killing, torture and mass rape by Burmese soldiers have been thoroughly documented by human rights groups and a United Nations fact-finding mission , external .

I have on many occasions interviewed ethnic Rakhine people about their animosity towards the Muslim population, and I have documented the systematic obliteration of what remained of Rohingya villages by the Myanmar state.

But the question posed at the UN's top court, the ICJ, is whether all of this amounted to genocide.

The ICJ was established in 1945 to help settle disputes between states, not to try international crimes. However, it was chosen to address the attacks on Rohingyas in Myanmar because there were few other avenues of redress for the victims.

Myanmar authorities have denied accusations of ethnic cleansing or genocide, saying they were only responding to terrorist actions by Rohingya militants with so-called military "clearance operations".

A UN report in 2018 , based on hundreds of interviews, said the army's tactics were "grossly disproportionate to actual security threats". It said top military figures in Myanmar must be investigated for genocide in Rakhine State and crimes against humanity in other areas. Myanmar rejected the report.

As Myanmar was not a signatory to the International Criminal Court, it was not possible to file a case there against the officials accused of atrocities in Rakhine State.

Instead in November 2019 The Gambia, backed by the Organisation of Islamic Co-operation, filed a case at the ICJ, arguing that all states are bound by the Genocide Convention, so all have an interest in upholding it.

It accused the state in Myanmar, not just the military, of genocide.

This was a novelty in international law; a state not directly affected by an act, arguing that it had legal standing to make a complaint because it was indirectly affected by any violations of such an important convention.

Myanmar objected to this argument, but the ICJ judges ruled that The Gambia was eligible to file the case.

The case drew even more attention when the Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi, who at the time headed the elected government in Myanmar, chose to lead the initial legal defence of her country at The Hague in person, for which she was widely criticised.

She had very limited influence over the actions of the Myanmar military in Rakhine State, but her refusal to condemn them dismayed many of those who until then had admired her courage and adherence to democratic principles.

Since she was deposed by a coup in 2021 and placed under arrest the defence has been led by a new team appointed by the military.

Historically, proving that genocide has been committed has been very difficult. Judges apply a high bar to this.

Typically, where there is no explicitly genocidal programme, like that of the Nazis, the judges require that the evidence presented at court must be such that the only reasonable inference from the actions of the defendants is that they had genocidal intent.

When Bosnia-Herzegovina filed a genocide case against Serbia at the ICJ in 1993, it took the court 14 years to conclude that while incidents like the 1995 massacre at Srebrenica did amount to genocide, there was not sufficient proof that the state of Serbia had genocidal intent, though it was found to have failed to prevent genocide.

Myanmar's lawyers and Aung San Suu Kyi have argued something similar.

Suu Kyi said that The Gambia's team mischaracterised a complex conflict and military operation, and that while she accepted that war crimes may have been committed against the Rohingyas, that is not proof of genocidal intent.

But Arsalan Suleman believes the weight of evidence his team gathered is enough to meet that high bar.

"What we presented to the court was the long history of discrimination targeting the Rohingya, and how that history, and the policies connected with it, provide a background to understand the government's language, rhetoric, propaganda, and policies that were part of the 2017 'clearance operations'," Suleman said.

"We discussed the 1982 citizenship law, and the tightening noose of discriminatory laws that restricted access to education, healthcare, livelihoods, and travel - all of which made life really impossible for the Rohingya and, we argued, was one of several indicators of genocidal intent."

What happens if the court does find in favour of The Gambia?

Myanmar would then find itself tarnished by having committed "the crime of crimes", as sitting on the same bench as Nazi Germany, the Rwandan Hutu militants and the Bosnian Serbs at Srebrenica.

That might seem a setback for Min Aung Hlaing, the general who now runs Myanmar, who above all was responsible for the military's operations in 2017, and who has been trying to improve his dismal international image in recent months.

There is no right of appeal against an ICJ verdict. However, there is also no penalty that follows an ICJ verdict.

The Burmese coup leader is focused mostly on rebuilding relations with neighbouring Asian countries, who are unlikely to pay too much attention to such a verdict, and much less on rebuilding relations with Western countries who do care.

But for the huge Rohingya diaspora this verdict matters a great deal.

"This is like formal recognition of our suffering," says Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who was driven out of the Rakhine town of Buthidaung in 2017 and now lives in Canada.

"For the Rohingya, this trial is a moment of acknowledgement of our suffering after years of denial. The Rohingya have been waiting for justice for decades, not just this year."

He and other Rohingya activists hope that a ruling in favour of The Gambia will prompt more co-ordinated action by other countries to find a resolution which allows them to go home to Rakhine State, in safety.

More than a million are stuck in wretched camps in Bangladesh, barred from employment as international funding dries up.

Rakhine State has been ravaged by a conflict between the military and the insurgent Arakan Army, which now controls most of the territory. It is supported by the indigenous Rakhine population who are very hostile to the idea of the Rohingyas coming back.

Many Rohingya villages have been completely destroyed. And international support for them has faded over the years. Even an unprecedented genocide verdict at the world's highest court cannot change that reality.

items.title: Israeli military launches rare ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
items.summary: Hamas condemns the incursion, which the Israeli military says is dismantling a "terror tunnel", as a "flagrant" ceasefire violation.
items.content:
Israeli ground forces have launched a rare operation in part of the central Gaza Strip outside their control, after issuing evacuation orders for residents.

Witnesses said tanks advanced east of Nuseirat refugee camp and rolled onto the territory's main north to south road under the cover of artillery strikes.

The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.

The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire agreement.

Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.

Early on Wednesday afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the incursion and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety.

It also said a section of the north to south Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.

Later, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had begun a joint operation with the Shin Bet security service "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".

"IDF troops under the Southern Command are deployed in the area in accordance with the ceasefire agreement and will continue to operate to remove any immediate threat and thwart attempts by the Hamas terrorist organisation to harm Israeli civilians or IDF troops, or to violate the agreement," it added.

Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".

Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the announcement.

In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man can be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he says.

Automatic gunfire can be heard in another video filmed just to the south-east.

A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter."

"We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind."

A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".

Asked about reported fatalities, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.

Israel building new land barriers in Gaza and displacing families

Israel moves Yellow Line deeper into Gaza, satellite images show

Gaza's Hamas-run Civil Defence agency said three people were killed and others were wounded in three separate Israeli drone strikes on Wednesday.

One man was killed in Nuseirat, the second to the north in Gaza City, and the third in the central town of Deir al-Balah, it added.

The IDF told the BBC that it had "struck several military operatives".

At least 1,658 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began last year, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

The Israeli military says six of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.

Meanwhile, more than 1.9 million people - about 90% of Gaza's population - remain displaced, with 1.4 million of them living in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN.

Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza, where an estimated 82% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, as US President Donald Trump's peace plan has largely stalled.

The group has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased withdrawal of Israeli troops from the 60% of Gaza they currently occupy. But Israel has insisted that Hamas must fully disarm before any pullout.

The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Since then, more than 74,700 people have been killed in Gaza, the health ministry says.

items.title: Catherine visits Mumbai maternity hospital on the last day of royal trip
items.summary: The Prince and Princess of Wales ended their three-day trip to India on Wednesday, the couple's first international tour since 2022.
items.content:
The Prince and Princess of Wales ended their three-day trip to India on Wednesday, the couple's first international tour since 2022.

Catherine visited a maternity hospital in Mumbai and was seen comforting a grieving mother who lost a baby after giving birth to premature twin girls.

William met actors Kareena Kapoor, Saif Ali Khan and filmmaker Karan Johar during a visit to a film production company.

The couple also met Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi, with a Kensington Palace spokesperson saying they discussed the "strength and importance of the UK–India bilateral relationship".

items.title: Il lusso sta cambiando, addio logomania, è la Legitimacy Era
items.summary: Qualità, autenticità e trasparenza diventano valori decisivi, i consumatori aspirazionali la forza del settore
items.content:
Il lusso sta cambiando: si acquista meno per esibire un marchio e sempre più per riconoscersi in un prodotto, apprezzarne la qualità o vivere un’esperienza capace di arricchire la propria vita. Un cambiamento che non riguarda soltanto la moda, ma il modo in cui le persone scelgono di spendere, attribuiscono valore agli oggetti e ridefiniscono il proprio rapporto con il benessere e il consumo.

A raccontare questa trasformazione è The Next Generation Platform (TNGP), gruppo di company specializzate in strategia, creatività e tecnologia, che attraverso il proprio lavoro interpreta l’evoluzione dei consumi e le nuove aspettative nei confronti dei brand.

I dati raccolti nell’ultima ricerca raccontano bene questa evoluzione: il 41% dei luxury spender acquista meno prodotti di lusso perché non ne riconosce più un valore adeguato al prezzo, mentre il 35% dei consumatori ha ridotto la spesa in beni di lusso a favore del wellness . E il mercato si apre anche a nuove forme di desiderabilità: un italiano su tre ha già acquistato un prodotto di lusso di seconda mano , privilegiando anche la storia, la durata e il valore di scoperta degli oggetti. E' una nuova fase: The Legitimacy Era, un momento in cui qualità, autenticità e trasparenza diventano decisive per riconquistare la fiducia dei consumatori. Una riflessione che va oltre il lusso e racconta un cambiamento più ampio nel modo di scegliere e attribuire valore. ANSA LIFESTYLE ha chiesto a Francesca Sonzini (Strategy, Content & Marketing Director) di spiegare meglio questa fase, che evoluzione del lusso racconta? "Finiscono gli anni di un lusso fatto di ostentazione dei loghi o di prestigio iper-esclusivo. Si superano anche gli anni del “quiet luxury”, in cui molti brand hanno scelto posizionamento ed estetica sobri, ma spesso omologati. I consumatori stanno ridefinendo le regole del desiderio, dell’accessibilità e del valore del lusso. Oggi un brand di lusso deve dimostrare di sostenere quel desiderio. La legittimità si costruisce su aspetti tangibili: qualità dei materiali, artigianalità, filiera trasparente e coerenza con la propria identità. Il 72% dei top-tier luxury spender dichiara di non trovare la qualità artigianale per cui paga (Forbes, 2025). Molti marchi di lusso devono tornare a guadagnarsi credibilità. Perché stiamo dicendo addio alla logomania? Perché possedere un logo non è più una tendenza così forte? "Perché il logo non ha più il valore di una volta, quando comunicava status attraverso l’ostentazion e. La sovraesposizione commerciale e la democratizzazione del lusso ne hanno diluito il prestigio. I consumatori oggi cercano il valore intrinseco del prodotto, con la qualità dei materiali al primo posto. Secondo Vogue Business (2025), il 41% dei luxury spender acquista meno lusso perché il prodotto non giustifica più il prezzo. Il desiderio si sposta verso pezzi unici, d’archivio, ed esperienze: Altagamma (2025) registra un +3% per il lusso esperienziale contro un -2% per i beni personali". Chi sono i luxury spender, come orientano oggi gli acquisti rispetto al passato? "Acquisiscono particolare centralità i consumatori aspirazionali, che secondo Ernst & Young) Europe (2026) sono la forza trainante della crescita del settore . Rispetto al passato sono focalizzati sulla sostanza: indagano processi, competenze e cultura dietro al prodotto. Sono più esigenti, l’80% si sente alienato dagli store sovraffollati, e cercano spazi dedicati e ad alto contatto umano (Forbes, 2025). Spostano le proprie preferenze d’acquisto: il 35% ha ridotto gli acquisti di lusso riallocandoli sul wellness (BCG x Altagamma, 2025). Il lusso si sposta dagli oggetti da possedere a tempi, luoghi ed esperienze da vivere. Questa tendenza riguarda solo l'Italia? "Si tratta di un cambiamento globale e l’Italia ne è un caso particolarmente vivace. Vale per esempio per il fenomeno del lusso pre-owned: secondo McKinsey e BoF, il second hand crescerà da due a tre volte più velocemente del nuovo fino al 2027, con l’Asia in testa e l’Europa in aumento del 12%. In Italia un consumatore su tre ha già acquistato lusso di seconda mano (EY, 2025) e Vinted ha raggiunto gli 11 milioni di membri registrati, dato fornito dal suo CEO a Il Sole 24 Ore".

items.title: Cobolli si arrende, Alcaraz irresistibile
items.summary: La rubrica Monday’s Net
items.content:
Come accade sempre alle ATP Finals da qualche anno in qua, vale la legge del più forte. Così, dopo Alexander Zverev , anche Carlos Alcaraz va diritto in semifinale: batte Daniil Medvedev 6-2 6-4 in poco più di un'ora, con sette giochi di fila a cavallo dei due set. Ora il tedesco e lo spagnolo devono solo chiudere i propri gironi e attendere i nomi degli avversari, che si sapranno domani e venerdì.

Nel giro di ventiquattr'ore il russo, numero 5 del mondo, e Ben Shelton , 4, non hanno mai dato l'impressione di poter competere con Carlitos e Zverev. Più che sconfitte, le loro sono apparse misurazioni reali della distanza abissale tra i tre capifila del ranking ATP (che al numero 2 vede Jannik Sinner) e tutti gli altri. L a classifica descrive infatti sommariamente il distacco tra il trio di testa e il plotone, con Zverev che assomma 9320 punti, l'italiano 7950, Alcaraz 6100, Shelton 5170, Medvedev 3820 . Ma lo spagnolo è rimasto fermo quattro mesi e mezzo a metà stagione per i problemi al polso e Sinner è alle prese da luglio con il tendine del ginocchio destro.

I dati agonistici danno indicazioni più chiare dei ranking. Dagli Australian Open del 2024 in tre hanno alzato le coppe dei dodici slam: cinque Sinner, altrettanti Alcaraz, e due Zverev, quest'anno . Non è una novità.

Il tennis moderno funziona così da quasi mezzo secolo: in cima c'è posto per due, al massimo per tre. Tra il 1978 e il 1981 Bjorn Borg e John McEnroe si affrontano quattordici volte, spartendosi equamente i successi. Si trovano l'uno contro l'altro in quattro finali slam in quattordici mesi: la prima è Wimbledon 1980, con il tie-break del quarto set che l'americano si prende 18-16 e il quinto set che va allo svedese. Le altre tre le vince McEnroe, fino agli UsOpen del 1981, dopo i quali Borg, a 25 anni, di fatto decide di smetterla con il tennis. Il terzo protagonista di quel decennio è Jimmy Connor s. Dal 1976 al 1984 nove Wimbledon di fila vanno a loro tre, dal 1978 al 1984 Connors e McEnroe si dividono sette Us Open consecutivi.

La seconda metà degli anni Ottanta è l'eccezione che allarga la regola senza smentirla. I padroni diventano quattro: Ivan Lendl, Mats Wilander, Stefan Edberg, Boris Becker . Tra il 1985 e il 1989 diciassette slam su diciannove sono roba loro. Dentro il quartetto, però, le gerarchie cambiano di stagione in stagione: Lendl gioca otto finali consecutive agli UsOpen, Wilander nel 1988 vince tre slam su quattro, Edberg e Becker si battono in tre finali di Wimbledon, una dopo l'altra.

Gli anni Novanta tornano alla formula della coppia in fuga. Pete Sampras e Andre Agassi si scontrano in trentaquattro match, venti li vince Sampras. Cinque finali slam, e quattro sono di Pete: la prima agli Us Open del 1990, l'ultima agli Us Open del 2002, che è anche l'ultima partita della sua carriera. Sampras chiude da numero 1 sei stagioni di fila, dal 1993 al 1998. Agassi nel 1997 scivola oltre la centoquarantesima posizione e poi risale fino in cima. Per un paio d'anni il ruolo di terzo incomodo tocca a Jim Courier, quattro slam tra il 1991 e il 1993.

Le epoche senza padroni non mancano, ma durano poco . Nel 2003 i quattro slam hanno quattro vincitori diversi: Agassi, Juan Carlos Ferrero, Roger Federer, Andy Roddick . L'8 settembre Ferrero diventa numero 1 e lo resta per otto settimane. È lo stesso Ferrero che domenica sedeva nel box di Shelton.

Poi arriva l'oligopolio più lungo. Dal Roland Garros del 2005 agli UsOpen del 2007 Federer e Rafael Nadal vincono undici slam consecutivi. Agli Australian Open del 2008 si aggiunge Novak Djokovic e i due diventano tre. Da Wimbledon 2003 agli UsOpen 2023 si giocano ottantuno slam: sessantasei sono loro, venti di Federer, ventidue di Nadal, ventiquattro di Djokovic. L'unico loro costante competitor è Andy Murray, e la sua carriera dice quanto costasse esserlo: undici finali slam, tre vinte, otto perse, tutte contro Djokovic o Federer . Diventa numero 1 nel novembre del 2016, ci resta quarantuno settimane, poi l'anca presenta il conto.Il trio di oggi è di ragazzi di 29, 25 e 23 anni, e l'anomalia è Zverev, che non è il giovane che si aggiunge a una coppia, come Djokovic nel 2008, ma un giocatore esperto che si colloca in cima dopo tre finali slam perse, agli UsOpen del 2020, a Parigi nel 2024, a Melbourne nel 2025: negli ultimi due casi contro gli altri due, Alcaraz e Sinner, che erano già lì. A Shelton resta da capire se sarà il Murray di quest'epoca. Ferrero è stato chiamato nel suo team per questo. Oppure potrebbe essere Rafael Jodar . Oppure nessuno.

Nel secondo singolare della giornata Flavio Cobolli ci prova, dà quello che ha, e non basta. Frances Tiafoe vince 7-6 6-0 , ma la seconda sconfitta in tre giorni non cancella quello che la stagione ha detto del romano: i margini per crescere ci sono, e sono ampi. Da adesso, per lui, conta l'appuntamento di venerdì. Lo aspetta Alcaraz , già qualificato per le semifinali, e nessuno dei due ha qualcosa da perdere. Potrebbe somigliare a un'esibizione, di quelle in cui ci si diverte: per Flavio, il modo migliore di salutare Torino.

È il quarto incontro della stagione tra Cobolli e Tiafoe . Il numero 2 d'Italia aveva vinto il più importante, la finale di Acapulco in marzo, il numero 2 d'America gli altri due, a Indian Wells e ad Halle . Il sintetico al chiuso della Inalpi Arena, veloce e con rimbalzi extra, è la superficie che il romano gradisce meno. Eppure parte con otto punti consecutivi e si porta sul 2-0, sereno e concentrato, senza risentire dell'infortunio che l'ha tenuto fermo proprio alla vigilia del torneo. Poi l'americano trova misura e ritmo, recupera il break, e a patire nei turni di servizio diventa l'italiano.

La carta in più di Flavio è il pubblico, che lo incoraggia con calore da stadio. Piace il suo stile gladiatorio. Nell'angolo ci sono il fratellone Matteo Berrettini e il capitano azzurro Filippo Volandri. Nel tie-break i cori - alè alè alè Flavio Flavio alè - lo portano fino a due palle del set. Tiafoe le annulla e chiude alla prima occasione.

Il secondo set comincia con un break e non ha più storia. Il linguaggio del corpo è esplicito: Flavio smette di crederci. È Berrettini a sostenerlo dopo ogni quindici, in piedi, urlando consigli (sarà un ottimo coach, tra qualche anno). Flavio prova a reagire, ed è anche sfortunato. Meriterebbe di prendersi un paio di game, ma non è giornata.

È una selezione che copre esigenze molto diverse: aggiungere Alexa in una stanza, portare le app di streaming su un televisore o passare a un lettore dedicato agli ebook. items.title: Torna il ReWriters Fest, Romanelli: 'Evento trasversale tra istituzioni e cultura pop'
items.summary: A Roma dal 19 al 22 novembre. Madrina Giordana Angi, a Vladimir Luxuria il Premio ReWriters 2026
items.content:
Torna a Roma dal 19 al 22 novembre, il ReWriters Fest , il primo evento in Europa interamente dedicato alla sostenibilità sociale. Giunta alla sua sesta edizione e ideata e diretta dalla giornalista, scrittrice ed imprenditrice Eugenia Romanelli con un team tutto al femminile, la rassegna si articola quest'anno su quattro giornate a ingresso gratuito, accessibile e plastic free, dividendosi tra la dimensione istituzionale dell'Auditorium Bnl Bnp Paribas (alla Stazione Tiburtina) e il cuore pop della Galleria Alberto Sordi e della sua Libreria Mondadori.

Ispirato ai 10 obiettivi sociali dell'Agenda Onu 2030 e al Manifesto etico di Rewriters.it, sostenuto da un comitato scientifico che annovera, tra gli altri, Massimo Recalcati e Lidia Ravera, il festival punta a tradurre in dibattito pubblico temi cruciali: dalla violenza economica e di genere all'omolesbobitransfobia, dalla salute mentale all'educazione sessuo-affettiva, fino a crisi climatica, intelligenza artificiale, sport inclusivo e giustizia intergenerazionale.

"Quest'anno il festival si allunga a quattro giornate e si divide in due anime: una più istituzionale, rivolta a imprese, istituzioni e terzo settore per aiutare il sistema Paese a posizionarsi sugli obiettivi dell'Agenda 2030, e una parte di intrattenimento che lavora sull'advocacy nella cultura pop. Politicamente è un festival trasversale, perché la dimensione sociale appartiene tanto alla tradizione culturale della destra quanto alla storia dei diritti della sinistra.

Mettere in dialogo soggetti che di solito non comunicano è la nostra sfida, resa possibile dal fatto che tutti partecipano senza cachet: non paghiamo per parlare di etica", spiega la Romanelli all'ANSA che è media partner del festival.

Tra gli ospiti attesi figurano volti del cinema, del giornalismo, della musica e dell'attivismo: da Anna Foglietta, Chiara Francini, Paola Minaccioni, Eva Grimaldi, Marco Bonini e Pietro Turano ai registi Enzo Monteleone e Riccardo Milani; dai giornalisti e conduttori Michele Santoro, Massimo Giannini, Francesca Fialdini, Eleonora Daniele, Antonio Padellaro, Gino Castaldo, Luca Telese, Maria Novella De Luca, David Giacalone, Salvo Sottile, Annalisa Bruchi e Antonello Dose fino ai cantautori Alex Britti e Annalisa Minetti.

Presenti inoltre Laura Boldrini, le scrittrici Romana Petri, Enrica Tesio e Chiara Tagliaferri, gli atleti Daniele Cassioli, Arturo Mariani, Eloisa Coiro e Maria Moroni, attivisti come Cathy La Torre, Imma Battaglia, Benedetta De Luca e Francesco Lepore, oltre a creator e divulgatori.

Madrina di questa edizione la cantante Giordana Angi mentre il Premio ReWriters 2026 sarà assegnato a Vladimir Luxuria: "La scelta di Giordana Angi come madrina va nella direzione di amplificare il messaggio, grazie al suo coming out importante e al grande pubblico che riesce a raggiungere. Vedere tante realtà salire a bordo dimostra che l'Italia è più avanti delle sue politiche", sottolinea Eugenia Romanelli.

Intanto si guarda già al futuro: "Ripeteremo sicuramente l'esperienza del ReWriters Fest XS a Cagli. I risultati della prima edizione sono stati stupefacenti: abbiamo raggiunto sedici milioni di persone e registrato il sold out per tre giorni consecutivi superando in proporzione le presenze fisiche di Roma. Questo dimostra che i territori hanno una fame enorme di partecipare al dibattito pubblico e che lo scambio intergenerazionale tra giovani e comunità locali funziona benissimo".

items.title: Can Anthropic's record breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?
items.summary: Anthropic's hotly anticipated IPO is expected to put it in the top 10 most valuable US companies, but the future is uncertain.
items.content:
It was during November 2020 that somewhere in San Francisco, a woman called Daniela Amodei phoned a friend, asking for advice.

Daniela oversaw safety and policy at OpenAI, one of the most talked-about AI companies in the world.

But Daniela and her brother Dario - who worked there too - had misgivings over safety levels at OpenAI and thought it could be time to walk away.

So she did what many do when we can't make a decision about something, she phoned a friend. The friend's reply was direct and to the point: "You don't need to be on the phone with me. You already know the answer."

The Amodei siblings and a handful of other colleagues quit. Together, they set up a rival – Anthropic.

Six years on and Anthropic, the maker of leading AI model Claude, has predicted revenues of $52bn in 2026 and $135bn in 2027, according to analyst estimates.

It is about to sell shares to the public for the first time in what's known as an Initial Public Offering or IPO, aiming for a valuation of an estimated $1.4tn (£1tn), which would propel it straight into the top 10 of the most valuable US companies.

The sale comes at a crucial time when many are wondering whether, amid increasing concern about the potential of AI, the industry's bubble is showing signs of bursting.

Where once investors were "all in" on a technological revolution to rival the railroads, the car, electricity and the internet, some are now hedging their bets, amid arguments that AI prices will be driven down as the technology becomes more common and concerns that a hefty wedge of the AI investment is tech giants investing in each other.

Shares in companies that supply the raw computing power behind AI, like Coreweave and Nebius, have seen their value cut in half while even the mighty Nvidia has lost its crown as the world's most valuable company with its shares down 30% - a staggering $2tn fall in value.

So could the Anthropic IPO reinflate the bubble or will it be remembered as the last gasp of a boom that is heading for a bust?

At an event last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told JPMorgan Chase's CEO Jamie Dimon that his guiding principle was to "never let your company be worth a single dollar more than it's worth".

The company is selling roughly $65bn worth of shares to the general public and a further $26bn on to other big tech companies. It is comfortably the single biggest money raising event in US corporate history.

It's an old adage that during a gold rush you should buy companies that sell the picks and shovels as opposed to those staking everything on striking gold. In AI's case that's the chip makers, the data centre builders, the energy providers. But Anthropic is arguably the gold itself and this IPO will see what value people put on it, according to Fiona Cincotta.

"I think the reason that this IPO is so important is basically it's the first ability for the public investors to access a pure play AI trade," she says, adding that previous offerings have been about "other parts of the ecosystem, which are, the semiconductors, the chips, the, data centres. But this is the first time that we were actually able to access the AI provider."

What a company is worth depends almost entirely on predicted future earnings.

It's that calculation that many think presents the sharpest needle to the AI bubble.

Will current and future users of AI be prepared to pay enough to justify the trillions being spent on the chips, data centres, energy and employees, some of whom can command annual salaries of over $100m?

"AI is certainly in a financial bubble. While LLMs [large language models] offer genuine utility and are undoubtedly here to stay, the economics don't add up," said Gary Marcus, Professor Emeritus at New York University and author of Taming Silicon Valley, speaking earlier this year.

"[The] more companies build AI models, the [more the] technology becomes commoditised, eliminating meaningful competitive advantages and driving down prices."

So far, the growth rates in Anthropic revenue are extraordinary.

But these explosive growth rates hide a potential problem. Around a quarter of that revenue came from just a handful of companies, among them Google and Amazon.

It's also concentrated in the US which accounts for two-thirds of its revenue.

There is also the staggering network of circular financing found in the AI world. For example, Anthropic has agreements to buy or lease hundreds of billions of dollars worth of chips and computing power from a handful of companies including Broadcom, Google, Amazon. Many of those firms are also investors in Anthropic and major customers of its products.

It's not just some Wall Street investors questioning whether the AI boom is all it's cracked up to be. Out on Main Street, ordinary Americans have concerns too.

With the US driving so much of global AI growth, a growing public backlash against a technology that threatens to replace millions of jobs and hoover up vast amounts of energy and water became a factor in the recent midterm elections in the US.

Many areas in the US have passed moratoriums on data centre development and many candidates deemed too close to big tech found that association a political liability rather than an asset. Many Democrat candidates publicly opposed data centre development and won.

Added to that, the Pied Piper of AI, chip maker Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang, resigned last week after admitting to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang.

Huang's spectacular fall from grace and Nvidia's 30% fall in value from its peak have left AI investors looking for a new champion for the AI boom that has underpinned the US stock market and arguably much of its entire economy for the last two years.

If Anthropic – and its CEO are to be AI's new Pied Piper, he will be playing a different tune to the relentlessly upbeat, leather jacket-clad talisman Huang.

While Huang wanted AI development to continue full throttle, Anthropic was built on misgivings over the levels of safety and responsibility the OpenAI leavers felt were being exercised over the development of society-changing technology.

Amodei has warned that AI capabilities could enable biological weapon development, mass surveillance, authoritarianism and the replacement of millions of white-collar, tax-paying workers.

He has called for a slowdown in its development as its powers are growing at such an exponential rate that it could very soon elude any human oversight.

That said, his paternalistic overtures have been sceptically received by those who point out that the pace of Anthropic's development of new more powerful models has shown no sign of the slowdown he's advocating for the rest of the industry.

But for all the concerns, just as with Elon Musk's SpaceX before it – the hype and the FOMO (fear of missing out) on an undoubtedly profound moment in technological and perhaps human development – means that buying interest is high.

It's reported that orders to buy shares exceed the number on offer by over six times.

With demand outstripping supply by such a margin, a first-day jump is likely given the oversubscription, but it doesn't tell you much about long-run return.

Using SpaceX as an example again, shares initially rose nearly 70% from its IPO sale price of $135 to $225. Shares in SpaceX are currently back to $145.

The Anthropic IPO could be wildly successful and blow a bit of fresh new air into what some maintain still looks a lot like a bubble.

Eileen Burbidge, founder of tech investors Passion Capital, is one of those who reject the notion that AI is a bubble about to burst.

"Maybe the growth of the bubble has slowed down a little bit, but actually I wouldn't be willing to say that it's about to burst yet," says Burbidge. "I think this IPO could actually mean everyone could be off to the races again."

Fiona Cincotta believes Anthropic's IPO is about far more than just Anthropic. "I think what's going to be really interesting here is I think it can actually be used as a valuation benchmark for the entire AI ecosystem," she says.

"That's why I don't think this is just going to affect the share price of Anthropic. I think this is going to have much wider implications across the whole AI trade."

Two things can be true at the same time. The Anthropic IPO could be wildly successful - FOMO is a powerful emotion in financial markets. But its probable success won't soothe the unease in some quarters that not every company, every investor and every citizen will think of AI as the answer to humanity's problems.

Atp Finals: Cobolli crolla con Tiafoe, sfumano le semifinali

Si ferma al primo turno la corsa di Flavio Cobolli delle Atp Finals di Torino.

Dopo la sconfitta con Medvedev l'azzurro ha perso anche con lo statunitense Frances Tiafoe.

Il punteggio finale è stato 7-6 (6) 6-0 in un'ora e 31 minuti di gioco. Per Cobolli - che nel primo set non è riuscito a concretizzare due palle set - è ora matematicamente impossibile qualificarsi alle semifinali.

items.title: Democrats nominate Hakeem Jeffries to be US Speaker of the House
items.summary: The nomination sets him on the path to become the first black lawmaker to lead the chamber when Democrats take control of the House in January.
items.content:
Democrats in the US House of Representatives officially nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be Speaker, setting him on the path to become the first black lawmaker to lead the chamber.

The House will elect its new Speaker on 3 January, when the next term begins and Democrats will be in the majority.

His election to the powerful position - the Speaker is in line to succeed the president after the vice-president - is widely expected. Should he win, Jeffries will preside over his party's largest House majority in years and benefit from the Senate also being under Democrats' control.

Jeffries told reporters after the vote that the nomination was "a high honour and a distinct privilege".

As of Wednesday, Democrats will hold at least 257 seats in the House next year, which is well beyond the 218 needed for a majority. Seven races from the recent midterm elections are still uncalled.

Jeffries, who represents a district in New York, was re-elected as the party leader in a 251-11 closed-door vote on Wednesday. He has served as minority leader since 2023.

The Congressional Black Caucus, currently made up of only Democratic House members, noted the potential history-making moment when Jeffries takes the helm of the House.

"The American people, largely driven by turnout among Black communities, particularly across the south, have trusted us to make Washington work for them," said the committee's chair, Yvette Clarke, in a statement. "Now, it is our charge and responsibility to do all we can to deliver on their faith."

Despite overwhelming support in Wednesday's vote , Jeffries faced a handful of holdouts from new members in the party's left wing, who have said the party's sweeping victory in the midterm elections is a sign voters want change.

"While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes in this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of our leadership," seven incoming lawmakers, including fellow New Yorkers Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, said in a statement.

All congressional Democrats are gearing up for clashes with the White House once they officially take control in January.

President Donald Trump, a Republican, has signalled a willingness to work with Democrats on some issues, but has also pledged to use his veto power to reject legislation he does not like.

Trump's opposition could make it hard for Democrats to deliver on their campaign promises to address affordability and pass other reforms.

At a news conference following the vote on Wednesday, Jeffries pledged that House Democrats would "fight to lower the high costs of groceries and gas and housing", and "make healthcare affordable for every single American".

Though the party will have a large enough majority to weather defections on must-pass legislation, Jeffries will still have to navigate internal ideological divisions that have grown particularly sharp over US support of Israel and Americans' rising healthcare costs .

Many incoming Democrats, including members of the Democratic Socialists of America, won their elections by challenging the party establishment.

The Congressional Progressive Caucus, from the party's left wing, congratulated Jeffries on the nomination, adding they would "continue conversations with Leader Jeffries to ensure Democrats deliver a bold agenda for working people".

Along with shepherding legislation, Jeffries as Speaker will also have to manage the complex array of investigations that Democrats plan to launch into Trump, his family, and cabinet members now that they have regained control of the chamber's oversight powers.

Rounding out their party leadership team, House Democrats also elected Katherine Clark of Massachusetts as majority leader, Pete Aguilar of California as majority whip, and Joe Neguse of Colorado as assistant speaker.
